title: How AI is changing Software Engineering: A Conversation with Gergely Orosz, @pragmaticengineer

summary: The conversation opens with 'token maxing,' a practice at large tech companies where engineers artificially inflate AI token usage metrics. Meta used a leaderboard and token counts as a performance evaluation data point; Microsoft saw junk code generation; Salesforce enforces a ~$175/month minimum AI spend. Leadership pressure drives adoption—Coinbase fired an engineer for non-use. Orosz compares this to discredited lines-of-code metrics and LeetCode interviews as cultural compliance selection. On productivity, individual gains are real but team-level improvements remain uncertain; a 30-person meter study found participants felt 20% more productive but were actually 20% less, with one outlier. Enabling non-technical collaborators to code may be the greater organizational unlock. Orosz notes AI is hard to master: it takes sustained practice, and understanding underlying theory does not improve practical usage—a break from compiler/assembly intuition. Teams succeeding with AI share low ego and openness to leaving priors behind. The software engineer role is shifting as testing, DevOps, and product responsibilities collapse into engineering; John Deere reports two-pizza teams becoming one-pizza teams. Orosz rejects the framing that engineers are now 'managers of AI agents,' likening orchestration to a tech lead or 'mech suit' role with faster feedback loops and no people management burden. Large companies like Uber, Airbnb, Meta, and Microsoft are building custom internal AI tooling—background coding agents integrated into monorepos, MCP gateways tied to service discovery, retooled on-call systems, and risk-categorized code review—driven by hands-on learning, codebase scale, and funding incentives. Shopify exemplifies heavy AI investment: first external Copilot user in 2021, giving unlimited budget and trading churn and expense for a several-month competitive edge. Shopify's CTO Farhan acknowledged cost concerns but justified spending for innovation and recruitment, noting it would look silly to deny engineers these tools. Orosz then recounts growing The Pragmatic Engineer, started as a COVID-era experiment after Uber layoffs hit his team. He found immediate product-market fit—100 paid subscribers before publishing anything, 1,000 within six weeks—and spent two years saying no to all collaborations to focus on writing. After two years he expanded into a team and podcast, reaching #1 paid technology newsletter status within four months and holding it for three years.

sections.title: What is token maxing?
sections.summary: Orosz explains token maxing: large companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Salesforce measure AI token output, sometimes via leaderboards. Engineers game these metrics by generating unnecessary AI interactions. Meta used token counts as one performance evaluation data point and removed its leaderboard after public criticism, but the practice persists due to layoff fears.

sections.title: Is AI-driven productivity worth the hype?
sections.summary: Orosz traces token maxing to leadership pressure for AI adoption, citing a CTO dinner and Coinbase firing an engineer for non-use. He compares it to LeetCode interviews as cultural selection for compliance. He notes individual AI productivity gains are real but team-level improvements are uncertain, and retrofitting AI into existing workflows is hard.

sections.title: Productivity studies and organizational unlocks
sections.summary: The interviewer cites a meter study showing participants felt 20% more productive but were 20% less, with one outlier in a 30-person sample. The interviewer suggests enabling non-technical collaborators to code with AI may be the real organizational unlock. Orosz recalls Simon Willison saying AI workflows remain difficult to master after two years with no manual.

sections.title: AI mastery, role changes, and the engineer-as-manager question
sections.summary: Orosz explains two counterintuitive aspects of AI: mastery takes sustained practice, and understanding theory does not improve practical usage. Successful teams share low ego and openness. The software engineer role is consolidating tester, DevOps, and product responsibilities; John Deere reports two-pizza teams becoming one-pizza teams. Orosz rejects the 'engineers are now AI managers' framing, likening orchestration to a tech lead or mech suit role with faster feedback loops and no people management. DHH and Michelle Hashimoto offer supporting analogies.

sections.title: Large tech infrastructure and internal AI tooling
sections.summary: Orosz describes how large companies—Uber, Airbnb, Meta, Microsoft—are rebuilding internal AI infrastructure: custom background coding agents integrated into monorepos, MCP gateways tied to service discovery, retooled on-call systems, and risk-categorized code review. Three drivers: low-risk hands-on AI practice, custom solutions outperforming vendors for massive codebases, and easy funding for AI-tagged projects.

sections.title: Shopify's early AI investment and churn
sections.summary: Shopify became the first external company to access GitHub Copilot in 2021 by trading feedback from 3,000 users for early access. The tool caused significant initial churn but Shopify persisted, illustrating why heavy AI investment in internal tooling can make strategic sense despite early friction.

sections.title: Shopify's AI strategy rationale and Pragmatic Engineer growth
sections.summary: Shopify gives unlimited budget for AI tools, trading churn and expense for a several-month competitive edge. CTO Farhan worries about cost but justifies it for innovation and recruitment, noting it would look silly to deny engineers tools they need to attract top talent. Everyone doing AI simultaneously makes it look silly but rational. Orosz then recounts starting The Pragmatic Engineer during COVID after Uber layoffs hit his team. He found immediate product-market fit: 100 paid subscribers at $100/year before publishing anything, 1,000 within six weeks—matching his old Uber salary. For two years he said no to all collaborations, focusing solely on writing articles. He then hired researchers, started a podcast, and became the #1 paid technology newsletter within four months, holding the position for three years.
